subject: selective
title: How the selective maths test works

scenes.heading: How the selective maths test works
scenes.sub: Smart pacing is worth marks on its own
scenes.say: The selective maths paper is about thirty minutes of multiple-choice problem solving, with no calculator. Knowing how to pace yourself can win you marks before you even start calculating.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A runner sets checkpoints so they don't go out too fast or too slow
scenes.science: You set question checkpoints so you reach the end of the paper
scenes.breaks: a runner can't skip a hard hill, but you can skip a hard question and come back to it.
scenes.say: Think of a runner in a long race. They plan checkpoints so they don't go out too fast or fall behind. You do the same with question numbers. The difference? A runner can't skip a hill, but you can skip a hard question and come back later.

scenes.heading: The one-minute rule
steps: Read and underline what is asked
Return at the end if time
scenes.say: Use the one-minute rule. Read the question and underline what it asks. If you can see a method, go. If you're stuck after about a minute, put down your best guess, mark the question, and move on. Come back at the end if there's time.

scenes.heading: Plan your pace
scenes.question: 30 questions in 30 minutes. Keep 3 minutes to check. How many seconds per question?
scenes.say: Thirty questions in thirty minutes, keeping three minutes to check. That leaves twenty-seven minutes, which is sixteen hundred and twenty seconds. Divide by thirty: fifty-four seconds per question.
scenes.caption: 30 questions in 30 minutes, keeping 3 minutes to check. That leaves 27 minutes = 1620 seconds. 1620 ÷ 30 = 54 seconds per question.

scenes.heading: Never leave a blank
points: Read the instructions on the day
scenes.say: Never leave a blank. A blank always scores zero. A random guess has a one in four chance, and if you cross out two options first, it's one in two. Just read the instructions on the day in case they say otherwise.

scenes.heading: Estimate to choose
scenes.question: Which is closest to 6.1 × 19.8 ÷ 3.9?  3, 30, 120 or 300
scenes.say: Estimation saves time. Which is closest to six point one times nineteen point eight, divided by three point nine? Round to six times twenty, divided by four. That's one hundred and twenty divided by four, which is thirty.
scenes.caption: Which is closest to 6.1 × 19.8 ÷ 3.9? Round to 6 × 20 ÷ 4. That's 120 ÷ 4 = 30.

points: Stuck after a minute? Guess and move
scenes.say: Quick recap. Plan your pace with checkpoints, use the one-minute rule, never leave a blank, and estimate to check. Now try the practice questions!
